title: The OptiCord study - Timing of umbilical cord clamping in babies born very early who need support with their breathing at the time of birth
official: Timing of umbilical cord clamping for very preterm infants needing resuscitation at birth. (OptiCord)
summary:
Background and study aims
In the UK, 1-2 in 100 babies (1-2%) are born at least 8 weeks early – i.e. before 32 weeks. It is very common for them to need extra support with their breathing to get their lungs and heart working well. This is known as resuscitation.
Babies born prematurely are usually cared for by a neonatal doctor who, when it’s needed, helps to gently support the baby to get used to life outside the womb. The doctor will sometimes open the baby’s airway and give some support to their breathing. This is commonly known as stabilisation.
Resuscitation also includes stabilising the baby but with additional airway and breathing support like giving several rounds of ventilation breaths, compressions to the baby’s chest and sometimes, giving the baby medicine to help them breathe and make the heart beat more strongly.
In babies born prematurely who are otherwise well, leaving them connected to the placenta by the umbilical cord for a bit longer after birth means they get extra oxygen, red blood cells and iron, helping their lungs and blood circulation settle better and improving their chances of survival in good health. This practice is called ‘delayed’ or ‘deferred’ cord clamping. However, we don’t know, in babies who need resuscitation, whether it is as helpful. Currently in the UK, when babies need immediate resuscitation, the standard approach is to clamp the cord at around 30-60 seconds, in line with national guidelines.  
We want to find out the best time to clamp the umbilical cord for very premature babies for better survival, health and development. We do not know the best time to clamp the umbilical cord and whether leaving the umbilical cord attached to the placenta longer than the current standard approach is more beneficial or not during resuscitation. This research question has been prioritised as important by health professionals, parents and researchers all around the UK. We aim to include around 2400 very premature babies in the UK who need resuscitation at birth.

Who can participate?
Babies who are born more than 8 weeks early and who need breathing support at the time of birth may take part in the OptiCord study. Hospitals all around the UK are taking part in the study. If a baby requires resuscitation, this will always begin as soon as possible. In half of the hospitals, the standard approach will be followed, and the cord will be clamped at around 30-60 seconds. The other half of hospitals will wait at least three minutes before clamping the cord, with resuscitation carried out at the bedside while the baby’s umbilical cord remains attached to the placenta. To compare hospitals fairly and scientifically, each hospital is randomly assigned to follow one of the two approaches and will use this same approach for all babies born at least 8 weeks early who require resuscitation while the study is running.

What does the study involve?
We want to compare babies who stay attached to the placenta for longer via the umbilical cord, with babies whose cords are clamped at around 30-60 seconds after birth. We are comparing these two approaches to see whether they make a difference to babies’ survival, health and development.
We also want to check other important outcomes for mothers and babies in the first few weeks after they are born and into early childhood. We want to keep a close eye on babies’ wellbeing, including monitoring for infections and ensuring their bowels, lungs, and eyes are developing as expected. We will also look at babies’ quality of life at 1 and 2 years corrected age, and their development at 2 years corrected age. We will record information about mothers’ health and wellbeing, including whether they needed additional support after birth. We also want to know what mothers felt about the approach to resuscitation and their birth experience.
If we find that one approach to umbilical cord clamping timing is more helpful for babies’ survival and health, then we will be able to recommend other very premature babies receive this in the future to give them a better start in life.

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating?
Taking part in the study may not directly benefit you or your baby, but the information may help doctors in the future choose the best way to manage the umbilical cord for very preterm babies who need extra help with their breathing at birth.
Like in any research study, it’s really important we keep mothers and babies safe. If your baby was born in a hospital taking part in OptiCord, we will collect some basic anonymised information on all babies born at least 8 weeks early who received resuscitation at the time of birth and are eligible to be included in the OptiCord study. This is very important as we have a duty to ensure everyone who had resuscitation and umbilical cord clamping is kept safe, and closely monitor the outcomes and care of mothers and babies. This anonymised data does not include your personal details (i.e. name, contact details). You and your baby will not be identified in anyway by the basic anonymised data we will collect. More details about the data that is being collected is on the OptiCord website www.opticord.ac.uk. We will ensure the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) is followed.
There are no known serious risks or disadvantages to agreeing for your and your baby’s data to be included in the study. Some people may find that completing the questionnaires takes a bit of time, which can feel like a burden. While completing your questionnaire, you may find that being reminded of the birth and the time you spent in hospital after your baby was born brings back difficult memories or feelings. Some people find this upsetting or unsettling. If this happens, support is available. You can find more information about the support available on this information sheet.
If you find it difficult to answer the questionnaires in English, you can ask someone who is confident in English to help you. This could be a family member or a friend. If you don’t have anyone who can help, your local research team can provide support to make sure you are able to complete the questionnaires comfortably.
If your hospital follows the approach of keeping the umbilical cord intact while providing breathing support, and if you and your partner choose to talk to a researcher about your experiences, talking about your baby’s resuscitation may feel emotionally difficult. Your local research team will support you throughout the process and make sure you and your partner are able to access the support you need.

Where is the study run from? 
The study is being organised by the University of Leeds (the Sponsor) and coordinated by the Nottingham Clinical Trials Unit (NCTU) at the University of Nottingham.

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for?
The study should start recruitment in December 2026 and is expected to recruit until October 2029.

Who is funding the study?
The funding for the study is provided by the National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR), which is the research part of the NHS. All research in the NHS is reviewed by an independent group of people, called a Research Ethics Committee, to protect your interests. This study has been reviewed and given a favourable opinion by a Research Ethics Committee.

Who is the main contact?
Mickey Lewis, Clinical Trial Manager, email is OptiCord@nottingham.ac.uk

interventions.name:
The OptiCord trial is a multi centre, two arm, unmasked, cluster randomised, parallel group superiority trial designed to evaluate two established approaches to umbilical cord management for very preterm infants requiring resuscitation at birth.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Site-level inclusion criteria:
Due to the nature of the cluster design, sites will meet the following inclusion criteria to participate: 
1.	Secondary care hospitals with Level 2 (Local Neonatal Unit) or Level 3 (Neonatal Intensive Care Unit) neonatal units
2.	Hospitals who agree to be randomised to either the intervention or comparator group* 
*Hospitals will be required to provide confirmation that they are committed and willing to be randomised to either group of the trial

Participant-level inclusion criteria:
1.	Very preterm infants born before 32 weeks’ GA who are deemed to require resuscitation within one minute of birth. Resuscitation is defined as per the UK Newborn Life Support (NLS) resuscitation guidelines: sites will rapidly (within 30 seconds) assess tone and colour, adequacy of breathing and heart rate (count) to determine whether the infant requires resuscitation as described by the guideline
2.	Infants born by vaginal, instrumental or caesarean birth are all eligible to participate if they are alive
2.1 at the onset or during spontaneous labour and birth or
2.2 at the onset or during induction, instrumental or caesarean birth
Exclusion criteria:
Participant-level exclusion criteria:
1.	Preterm infants with a known lethal fetal anomaly (e.g. Trisomy 18, anencephaly)
2.	A known risk such as a fetal abnormality other than preterm birth that could adversely affect neurodevelopment at 2 years, e.g. chromosomal or genetic syndrome, brain abnormality
3.	Monochorionic multiple births*
4.	Triplets or higher-order multiple births
5.	Ruptured vasa praevia
6.	Umbilical cord accidents, e.g. snapped cord, lack of cord integrity, true knot
7.	Maternal resuscitation required in the case of massive acute maternal haemorrhage where the senior obstetrician determines that the intervention may impede maternal resuscitation efforts
8.	Fetal hydrops known at the start of labour or delivery
*Dichorionic twins are not excluded from participation in the trial. Should only one infant from a dichorionic pair be deemed eligible for participation, then the eligible infant should be considered for inclusion. In such a circumstance, the care for the non-eligible sibling is at the discretion of the assessing clinician and is not dictated by trial processes or procedures. In the case of DCDA twins, if one twin has demised > = 12 weeks of gestation, they are excluded. If the demise is before 12 weeks (& 0 days) of gestation (i.e. vanishing twin), the other twin can be included
